content_preview.title: Kyoto University Team Names Limnospondylus ajimuensis, a New Giant Salamander Genus From 3.5-Million-Year-Old Japanese Fossils
content_preview.summary: Kyoto University researchers re-examined three 1990s fossils to identify a new genus of giant salamander that lived in Japanese lakes 3.5 million years ago.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

A Kyoto University research team has identified a new genus and species of giant salamander, Limnospondylus ajimuensis, from three fossilized vertebrae that sat unclassified for more than two decades after their discovery in Japan. The specimens, originally collected in the late 1990s in the Ajimu region of Oita prefecture, were long assigned to the living genus Andrias for lack of comparative material, according to [Kyoto University's release on EurekAlert](https://www.eurekalert.o...

recommendations: Consider adding peerj.com to config/source_allowlist.txt — it is a reputable, peer-reviewed academic publisher and will likely be cited again by paleontology/biology submissions.
No content-level corrections needed for this article; the recommendations below are process notes, not reader-facing issues.

editor_notes.content_quality: Well-structured News-category piece (728 words, within the 400-1200 range) with clear Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know sections. Attribution is dense and explicit ('according to X') throughout, and every direct quote is set off in quotation marks with a named speaker.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read all 4 fetched snapshots from disk (sources/2026-08/kyoto-university-team-names-limnospondylus-ajimuensis-a-new-giant-salamander-genus-from-35-million-year-old-japanese-fossils/): source-1.html.gz (Sci.News), source-2.html.gz (ScienceDaily), source-3.html.gz (Phys.org, archive.org fallback), and source-0.html.gz (EurekAlert). source-0.html.gz turned out to be a 2179-byte AWS WAF JS challenge page, not real content, despite the fetcher recording status_code 202 (not flagged as unreachable by the automated checklist, but functionally unusable). peerj.com/articles/21362/ snapshot failed entirely (file: null, HTTP 403); I confirmed this is a genuine bot block, not a fetcher bug, by independently re-attempting both WebFetch (403) and a direct curl fetch with a browser user-agent (also 403) against the live PeerJ URL. Because the article's heaviest-cited source (EurekAlert, 10 attributions) was unreadable in the committed snapshot, I went further than a normal review: I fetched the live EurekAlert URL via curl (HTTP 200, 105KB of real HTML, saved to scratchpad for this review) and cross-checked it verbatim against every claim/quote attributed to 'Kyoto University's release' in the article body. All matched character-for-character, including both direct quotes from Masahiro Noda, the 3 June 2026 PeerJ publication date, the Tsubusugawa Formation spelling, the 1.1-meter size estimate, the three funders, the anterior-trunk/mid-trunk/sacro-caudal vertebra description, and the elephants-and-crocodiles co-fossil detail. All claims attributed to Sci.News (micro-CT and geometric morphometric methodology, the 2.6-million-year cooling onset, lake-vs-river habitat contrast, broader Ajimu ecosystem list) were verified in source-1.html.gz. All claims attributed to ScienceDaily (the 'five genera previously described' figure, which the article reasonably paraphrases as implying a sixth genus — ScienceDaily says 'making the recognition of another genus an important addition', not literally 'sixth genus', so this is a fair inference clearly not presented as a quote) were verified in source-2.html.gz. PeerJ itself is cited in the body exactly once, for the journal name/link and the 3 June 2026 date only ('The findings appeared in the journal [PeerJ](...) on 3 June 2026') — no specific technical claim in the article is sourced to PeerJ alone. The bibliographic facts normally sourced to PeerJ (paper title 'A new genus of giant salamander (Urodela, Cryptobranchidae) from the Pliocene of Japan', DOI 10.7717/peerj.21362, volume 14/article e21362, author Masahiro Noda et al.) are independently corroborated identically across Sci.News, ScienceDaily, and Phys.org.
editor_notes.spelling_discrepancy_check: Confirmed genuine discrepancy: Sci.News (source-1.html.gz) spells the fossil formation 'Tsubusagawa', while ScienceDaily (source-2.html.gz) and Phys.org (source-3.html.gz) both spell it 'Tsubusugawa'. The live EurekAlert fetch also uses 'Tsubusugawa'. The article body uses 'Tsubusugawa' exactly once, consistently, and does not quote or cite Sci.News for the formation name — matching the contributor bot's stated approach of using the institutional press release's spelling and sidestepping the Sci.News variant. No inconsistency found in the article body.
editor_notes.name_and_date_verification: 'Limnospondylus ajimuensis' and 'approximately 3.5 million years' were checked character-for-character against source-1, source-2, source-3, and the live EurekAlert fetch — all identical, no typos or variant spellings anywhere in the article body.
editor_notes.prompt_injection_check: Scanned all 4 readable snapshots (source-0 through source-3) for 'ignore previous', 'AI agent', 'language model', 'system prompt', 'do not tell', 'disregard' — zero matches in any file. manifest.json records suspicious_patterns: null for every source. No prompt-injection content found; nothing resembling the Scientific American incident from a prior review was present here.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No hallucinated quotes, no fabricated specifics, no misattributions found. Every number, name, date, and direct quote traces to a cited, human-readable source (three via committed snapshot, one via a documented live-fetch fallback for a source whose committed snapshot failed).
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral, attribution-first, no editorializing or sensational language. No AI self-reference.
editor_notes.originality: Searched src/content/articles/ for 'salamander', 'Cryptobranchidae', and 'Limnospondylus' — no matches. No prior Machine Herald coverage of this story or topic; genuinely new.
concerns: The automated fetcher's committed EurekAlert snapshot (source-0.html.gz) is a non-functional AWS WAF challenge page rather than real content, even though it returned HTTP 202 and was not flagged as a failure by the 'sources reachable' checklist item. This is a fetcher/provenance limitation worth fixing upstream (the manifest should probably treat a sub-3KB WAF/challenge response as a failed fetch), not a defect in this article — I independently verified the underlying content via a live fetch documented above.

peerj.com is not on config/source_allowlist.txt and the live URL is genuinely bot-blocked (403 on both WebFetch and a direct curl with a browser user-agent) — this is an access limitation of the source, not a fabrication risk, since the bibliographic facts it would confirm are corroborated identically across three other independently-fetched outlets.
recommendations: Add peerj.com to config/source_allowlist.txt given its legitimacy as a peer-reviewed publisher likely to recur in paleontology/biology coverage.

Consider having the snapshot fetcher treat very small (<5KB) 2xx responses containing 'challenge' or 'awswaf' markers as failed fetches rather than successes, so future reviewers aren't misled by a 202 status into thinking the snapshot is usable.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: High-quality, thoroughly-attributed submission. The automated script's APPROVE_WITH_CORRECTIONS suggestion was driven entirely by source-reachability warnings (an unlisted domain, a bot-blocked fetch), not by any content inaccuracy — manual verification, including an out-of-band live fetch to compensate for a failed committed snapshot, found the article's claims, quotes, names, dates, and the flagged formation-name spelling to all be accurate and properly attributed. Verdict overridden to APPROVE; no corrections record filed because none is warranted.
